chapters.title: Chapter 4: The Legal, Regulatory and Tax Basics in India

lessons.title: Routes to Invest: Direct Cheques, Syndicates and SEBI Angel Funds

children.text: You have found a startup you like and said yes. What happens next? Too many first-time angels send money after a WhatsApp chat and a thumbs-up emoji, then wait months without a single document proving they own anything. In Chapter 1 you saw the routes into deals. This lesson is about the plumbing: the exact steps and paperwork when you invest directly, where your money and shares actually sit in a syndicate, and how the journey works through a SEBI-registered angel fund.

body.text: Your investment is only as real as its paperwork. If you cannot point to signed agreements, an allotment filed with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, and shares or fund units recorded in your name, you do not yet own anything.

children.text: Route 1: Writing a Direct Cheque

markDefs.definition: A short, mostly non-binding document summarising the key terms of an investment: amount, valuation, instrument and main rights.
Share Subscription Agreement: the contract under which the company agrees to issue shares to you for a stated price.
Shareholders' Agreement: the contract setting out rights and obligations among shareholders, such as board seats, information rights, transfer restrictions and exit clauses.

children.text: When an Indian private company issues new shares to you, it is making a private placement under Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013. The rules are specific, and each step leaves a paper trail you should be able to see. It usually starts with a
term sheet
and ends with shares in your name, with an
SSA
and
SHA
in between.
Term sheet.
Agree the headline terms: amount, valuation, instrument and your key rights.
Due diligence.
Check the company's MCA records, financial statements, GST filings, existing cap table and any legal disputes.
Definitive agreements.
Sign the SSA and SHA, or a shorter combined agreement in small rounds.
Valuation and approvals.
The company obtains a valuation report supporting the issue price, its board approves the issue, and shareholders pass a special resolution.
Offer letter.
You receive a private placement offer letter in Form PAS-4, addressed to you by name.
Payment.
You pay from your own bank account through banking channels, never in cash. The company must keep the money in a separate bank account until shares are allotted.
Allotment.
The company must allot your shares within 60 days of receiving your money. If it cannot, it must refund you within the next 15 days, failing which interest at 12% a year applies from the 61st day.
Filing and credit.
The company files a return of allotment in Form PAS-3 within 15 days, and your shares are credited to your demat account or issued as a share certificate.

Under Rule 9B of the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules, 2014, private companies other than small companies must issue securities only in dematerialised form, with a compliance deadline that was extended to 30 June 2025. From 1 December 2025, a small company is one with paid-up capital of up to ₹10 crore and turnover of up to ₹100 crore. Many early-stage startups fall within those limits, so you may still receive a physical share certificate. Either way, keep your demat statement or original certificate safe: it is your proof of ownership when you eventually sell.

body.text: Never pay investment money into a founder's personal bank account or personal UPI ID, however trusted they are. The Companies Act requires subscription money to come through banking channels into the company, held in a separate account until allotment. Money sent to an individual is legally a payment to that person, not an investment in the company.

body.title: When allotment is late
body.prompt: A startup receives your ₹10 lakh but fails to allot shares within 60 days, and it only refunds you on day 90. Interest at 12% a year applies from day 61. Using simple interest, a 365-day year and 30 days of interest (days 61 to 90), how much interest are you owed, in rupees?
body.explanation: ₹10,00,000 × 12% × 30 ÷ 365 = ₹9,863. The rule exists to stop companies from sitting on investors' money indefinitely. In practice, the bigger issue is what a late allotment tells you about how the company handles compliance.

children.text: Route 2: Syndicates, and Where Your Shares Actually Sit

markDefs.definition: Special Purpose Vehicle: a company or LLP set up to hold one investment on behalf of several people, so the startup's cap table shows one shareholder instead of many.

children.text: "Investing through a syndicate" can describe very different legal set-ups. Before you transfer anything, ask exactly who will be the shareholder on the startup's records. There are three common answers: you directly, a SEBI-registered fund, or an
SPV
or nominee that holds shares for the whole group.

body.caption: Three ways a syndicate can hold your investment
headers: Who appears on the startup's cap table

cells: You, by name, alongside every other backer
Shares in your own name, with your own SSA or deed of adherence to the SHA
Private placement offers are limited to 200 persons per financial year, with some exclusions, and founders may resist a crowded cap table
SEBI-registered angel fund or other AIF
Units of the fund, backed by its investment in the startup
New angel funds accept only accredited investors; check the fund's registration and fees
A company, LLP or individual holding shares for the group
An interest in the SPV, or a private arrangement with the nominee
Weaker rights, unclear regulatory status when money is pooled from many people, and dependence on whoever controls the vehicle

body.title: Shares in your name vs units in a fund

columns.label: Shares in your name
points: Your ownership is recorded directly with the company and the MCA
You can exercise shareholder rights yourself
More paperwork for you on every deal
You manage records, tax reporting and any eventual sale

columns.label: Units in a SEBI-registered fund
points: The fund is the shareholder; you own a share of the fund
The manager exercises rights and handles paperwork
SEBI oversight of the fund, its disclosures and its manager
Fees and carry, and your money moves on the manager's timeline

children.text: Route 3: Investing Through a SEBI Angel Fund

markDefs.definition: The agreement between you and an AIF setting out your commitment, how drawdowns work, fees, distributions and your rights as an investor.

children.text: The angel fund route swaps paperwork for structure. You sign one
contribution agreement
with the fund instead of a new set of documents with every startup. The typical journey:

body.title: Your journey through a SEBI-registered angel fund

events.title: Get accredited
events.description: Apply to a SEBI-recognised accreditation agency with KYC and income or net worth proof. Since September 2025, new angel funds accept only accredited investors.

events.title: Onboard with the fund
events.description: Complete KYC with the fund, read its private placement memorandum, and sign the contribution agreement.

events.title: Commit capital
events.description: Agree how much you are prepared to invest. The fund needs at least five accredited investors before its first close.

events.title: Deals and drawdowns
events.description: As the fund backs startups, it draws down money from investors. An angel fund can invest between ₹10 lakh and ₹25 crore in any one startup.

events.title: Holding period
events.description: The fund generally holds each investment for at least 1 year, reduced to 6 months if it exits by selling to a third party.

events.title: Statements and distributions
events.description: You receive periodic valuations and reports, and cash comes back to you when the fund exits an investment.

body.label: Tax treatment of Category I AIFs, including angel funds
body.context: Income other than business income is generally taxed in the hands of investors, not the fund. The next lesson covers how capital gains from angel investments are taxed.

body.label: MCA Portal: View Company Documents
body.description: Check a company's filings on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs portal, including whether a return of allotment has been filed after you invest.

body.title: The UPI request
body.question: A founder asks you to send your ₹5 lakh investment to his personal UPI ID "because the company's current account is still being set up". What is the core problem?
options: UPI transactions have a daily limit, so ₹5 lakh may need two days
Private placement money must reach the company through banking channels and be kept in a separate account until allotment; a personal transfer is not an investment in the company
There is no problem as long as the founder signs a receipt
body.explanation: Under Section 42, subscription money must be paid to the company through banking channels and held in a separate bank account until shares are allotted. A transfer to the founder personally gives you no claim to shares. Wait until the company account exists.

body.title: Dev's missing shares
body.scenario: Five months ago, Dev, an IT professional in Noida, joined a WhatsApp "angel syndicate" run by a former colleague and transferred ₹8 lakh to the colleague's LLP to invest in a D2C skincare startup. All he has is a Google Form confirmation. He checks the startup's filings and finds no allotment to the LLP or to him. His former colleague says "the paperwork is in progress".
body.prompt: What should Dev do now, and what should he do differently next time?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Ask in writing for specific documents: proof the LLP transferred money to the startup, the SSA or SHA the LLP signed, the startup's PAS-3 filing, and a document showing Dev's interest in the LLP.
2. Contact the startup directly to confirm whether it received any money from the LLP and whether shares were allotted.
3. If the answers are vague or there is no trace of money reaching the startup, send a formal written demand for a refund, and consult a lawyer about a legal notice. If there are signs of deliberate misuse, a complaint to the police or the Economic Offences Wing may be appropriate. SEBI's grievance systems will not help much if the vehicle was never SEBI-registered.
4. Next time: confirm before paying exactly who the shareholder will be; pay only the company or a SEBI-registered fund; insist on signed agreements and a PAS-4 offer letter first; and check the PAS-3 filing after the 60-day allotment window.
5. The lesson: informal pooling through a friend's LLP gives you the risks of angel investing without the legal protections.

body.title: Name the form
body.textWithBlank: After allotting shares in a private placement, a company must file its return of allotment with the MCA in Form ___ within 15 days.
body.explanation: Form PAS-3 reports the allotment to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs. The offer letter you receive before investing is Form PAS-4.

cards.definition: A short, mostly non-binding summary of an investment's key terms.
Share Subscription Agreement: the contract for the company to issue shares to you at a stated price.
Shareholders' Agreement: sets out rights among shareholders, such as information rights, transfer restrictions and exit clauses.
The private placement offer letter addressed to a named investor.
The return of allotment a company files with the MCA within 15 days of allotting shares.
Shares must be allotted within 60 days of receiving money, or the money refunded within the next 15 days.
A company or LLP that holds one investment on behalf of several people.
Your agreement with an AIF covering commitment, drawdowns, fees and distributions.

points: A direct investment is a private placement under Section 42: term sheet, diligence, SSA and SHA, approvals, PAS-4 offer letter, payment, allotment and PAS-3 filing.
Pay only the company, through banking channels, never a founder personally or in cash.
Shares must be allotted within 60 days of receiving your money, or refunded within the next 15 days, with 12% interest from day 61 if the refund is late.
In a syndicate, always ask who appears on the cap table: you, a SEBI-registered fund, or an SPV or nominee.
SEBI angel funds replace deal-by-deal paperwork with one contribution agreement, but new funds accept only accredited investors and charge fees and carry.
Check the company's MCA filings after you invest; a missing PAS-3 is a serious warning sign.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. Company law, SEBI and FEMA requirements are detailed, have exceptions and change over time, and non-resident investors face additional rules covered in the next lesson. Dev and the examples are illustrative. Consult a qualified legal professional and a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
